name: Pinealon
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A three-amino-acid peptide sold for the brain. Protective in rat hypoxia models; two small Russian reports in head-injury patients.
overview.lede: Pinealon is the Khavinson institute's tripeptide Glu-Asp-Arg. Despite the name, the institute says it was derived from Cortexin, a brain-cortex extract, not the pineal gland. It has the largest preclinical file in the family and two small Russian studies in people with old head injuries. In Russia it is a dietary supplement; it is not a registered medicine anywhere.

stats.lbl: amino acids: Glu-Asp-Arg, derived from the brain extract Cortexin
head-injury patients in the two Russian reports (a saline-controlled study and an uncontrolled series, possibly overlapping)

stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

mechanism.intro: A short peptide said to help neurons survive low oxygen and injury by switching on protective genes.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The 2016 computer model places Pinealon on the DNA sequence "ttcc" with "very strong" predicted binding; a 2021 review proposes binding sites in the PPARA and PPARG gene promoters. Docking calculations, not measurements in brain tissue.

parts.name: What the animal work showed
parts.text: Rats pre-treated for five days survived severe low pressure longer (184 versus 72 seconds to respiratory arrest; 10 per group). In rats with brain trauma about twice as many could learn an avoidance task at 96 hours. Cultured neurons from Alzheimer's and Huntington's mouse models regained dendritic spines; no human study in either disease exists.

more.title: More: the two human reports
paras: The U.S. patent (2013): 25 people aged 31–60 with symptoms one to ten years after a head injury, randomised to the peptide or saline for ten days; "good" results in 59.4%, a figure that cannot be produced from 25 people, and control results unreported. A 2021 institute review cites 72 patients on oral Pinealon who reported better memory and fewer headaches, with no control group or design given.

results.headline: Convincing-looking rat hypoxia data, encouraging cell models, and human reports that cannot be checked.
results.lede: The deepest preclinical record in the family, almost entirely from the institute and its St Petersburg collaborators. The human data are two small Russian reports.

stats.lbl: time to respiratory arrest in rats under acute hypobaric hypoxia, Pinealon versus control (10 per group)
"good clinical result" among 25 head-injury patients in the patent; controls' results not reported

items.t: Rat cerebellar neurons stressed with hydrogen peroxide or NMDA: less reactive-oxygen build-up. Neurons from Alzheimer's and Huntington's mouse models: more dendritic spines. Isolated crayfish neurons: survival after axotomy 13.7 versus 11.9 hours. Rat cortex explants: 37% larger area (patent).

Rats, acute hypobaric hypoxia: respiratory arrest at 184 versus 72 seconds, 10 per group (2008). Offspring of rats exposed to hypoxia in pregnancy: more survivors (14 versus 9 per female) and more active behaviour. Brain trauma (24 rats) and spinal trauma (27 rats): better learning, motor function and tissue appearance (patent). Toxicity tests in 72 mice, 65 rats and 84 guinea pigs: none reported.

25 adults with remote consequences of head injury, randomised to peptide or saline for ten days (patent, 2013): good result 59.4%, attention-test errors 12.6 to 6.4, EEG alpha index 35.7 to 47.9; control results unreported. 72 patients on oral Pinealon plus standard care (cited in Molecules 2021): better memory, fewer headaches; no design given.

more.title: More: why the rat data do not settle anything
paras: The 2008 hypoxia paper is the best-documented experiment in the family: ten rats per group, a clear outcome, a significant difference for Pinealon alone among four peptides. But its table and text disagree on the death rate, it has not been repeated outside the institute's circle, and surviving a vacuum chamber is not a human disease. The Alzheimer's claims are cell-culture observations.

effects.headline: Ten days of exposure in a few dozen Russians, no adverse-event table, and rodent toxicity tests in a patent.
effects.lede: The patent states "no negative effect" was registered in its 25 patients without describing how adverse events were sought. Rodent testing reported no toxic reactions.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not reported in either human study.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Very little. The peptide is reported to change antioxidant enzymes, serotonin-related gene expression and the stress-signalling enzyme ERK in rat neurons. What months of that does in a human brain is unmeasured.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Mood, sleep, seizures and cognition, since the rat data show it changes neuronal signalling; immune reactions to an injected peptide of uncertain purity.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: In rats: longer survival under hypoxia, better recovery from brain and spinal injury. In cells: more dendritic spines in dementia models. In two small Russian head-injury series: self-reported memory and headache improvements without usable controls.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
New confusion, seizures, severe headache or one-sided weakness
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Pinealon in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

stats.lbl: length of the only controlled human exposure, in 25 head-injury patients

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Pinealon.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Pinealon, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: One small saline-controlled study in a patent, one uncontrolled series in a review. Nothing registered.
trials.lede: A 25-patient randomised comparison with saline in a 2013 U.S. patent, and a 72-patient uncontrolled series cited in a 2021 institute review.

more.title: More: how the human studies were run
paras: Patent: 25 adults randomised to peptide or saline for ten days, with attention tests and EEG before and after; group sizes, control results and a "commonly used medications" comparison group in the tables are not described. The 72-patient series is known only from a sentence in the review.

running.title: Trials that have been run
items: Remote consequences of head injury, 25 adults, ten days, saline control, randomised (patent, 2013): "good" result 59.4%, better attention scores and EEG alpha index; control results unreported; not peer reviewed.
Post-traumatic brain symptoms, 72 patients, oral Pinealon plus standard therapy (cited in Molecules 2021): memory and headache improvements; no control group described.
No trial on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).

find.text: Search the registry for "Pinealon" and its sequence "EDR". We found no registered trial.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. A dietary supplement in Russia, a "research chemical" everywhere else.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine. The Russian drug directory RLS lists Пинеалон as a food supplement (БАД), an additional source of peptides of arginine, glutamic acid and aspartic acid. Supplements are registered on safety paperwork, not proof of effect.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Pinealon the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.
The name suggests the pineal gland; the institute says the peptide came from Cortexin, a brain-cortex extract. Melatonin or sleep claims attached to the name have no study behind them.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Pinealon, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: In Russia the same name is a food supplement; that says nothing about what is in a vial sold abroad under it.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
New confusion, seizures or severe headache
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.
